tokyo.name: Ueno Park
tokyo.summary: Tokyo's big public park, home to the Tokyo National Museum, Ueno Zoo, Shinobazu Pond and some of the city's best cherry blossom.
tokyo.expect: Wide paths, museums and shrines spread over a large area; packed with picnic parties in late March and early April.
tokyo.tip: Walk down to Ameyoko market under the railway tracks for street food afterwards.
tokyo.why: Opened in 1873 as one of Japan's first public parks, it gathers several of the country's major museums in one place.
flow: Enter from Ueno Station's park exit.
Walk past the museums to Toshogu Shrine.
Finish at Shinobazu Pond and Bentendo hall.
tokyo.best: Cherry blossom season or a weekday morning
tokyo.bestFor: Museums, shrines and a slow walk in one district

tokyo.name: Harajuku and Takeshita Street
tokyo.summary: The narrow street of youth fashion, crêpe stands and character shops next to Meiji Jingu, leading into the calmer lanes of Ura-Harajuku and Omotesandō.
tokyo.expect: Shoulder to shoulder on weekends; the side lanes and Cat Street are quieter.
tokyo.tip: Pair it with Meiji Jingu first thing, then walk Takeshita Street before noon.
tokyo.why: It is the place where Tokyo street fashion has been made and shown since the 1980s.
flow: Start at the Harajuku Station end.
Cross to Cat Street and down to Omotesandō.

tokyo.name: Golden Gai and Omoide Yokochō
tokyo.summary: Two pockets of postwar Shinjuku: Omoide Yokochō's smoky yakitori alleys by the station and Golden Gai's maze of tiny bars seating six or eight.
tokyo.expect: Many Golden Gai bars charge a seating fee and some are regulars-only; look for signs welcoming visitors.
tokyo.tip: Eat skewers in Omoide Yokochō around 7pm, then walk ten minutes to Golden Gai after 9pm when the bars fill.
tokyo.why: They are among the last surviving black-market-era alleys in central Tokyo, a contrast to the neon towers around them.
flow: Start at Omoide Yokochō by Shinjuku Station west exit.
Pick a bar in Golden Gai.
tokyo.bestFor: A night out in old Shinjuku

kyoto.name: Sanjūsangen-dō
kyoto.summary: A 120 m wooden temple hall holding 1,001 gilded statues of Kannon in long rows, with 28 guardian deities in front.
kyoto.expect: Shoes off and no photos inside; the hall is cool and dim, and a visit takes under an hour.
kyoto.tip: Combine it with the Kyoto National Museum across the road.
kyoto.why: It is the longest wooden building in Japan, and the massed statues date mostly from the 13th century.
flow: Walk the length of the hall past the 1,001 Kannon.
See the large seated Kannon at the centre.
Walk the outer veranda where archery contests were held.

seoul.name: Insadong
seoul.summary: Seoul's old arts quarter, with galleries, tea houses, calligraphy and craft shops along one main street and its alleys.
seoul.expect: Busy at weekends when the main street is closed to cars; Ssamziegil's spiral of small shops is the centre.
seoul.tip: Walk from Gyeongbokgung or Bukchon and stop at a traditional tea house in the side alleys.
seoul.why: It has been the city's centre for antiques and traditional crafts since the Joseon era.
flow: Walk the main street to Ssamziegil.
Duck into the alleys for a tea house.
